title: Incendium Amoris
description: Richard Rolle's principal Latin treatise (c. 1340–43), an autobiographical and doctrinal account of the contemplative life as he himself had experienced it: the warmth of divine love (calor), its sweetness (dulcor), and its song (canor), with instruction on prayer, meditation, and the discernment of spirits. The founding text of the English mystical tradition.
plot_or_argument: Rolle recounts his own conversion and his experience of the three degrees of love — fire, sweetness, and heavenly song — defends the contemplative life against its critics, and teaches the reader to progress from reading through prayer to the 'fire of love' that unites the soul to God.
narrative_structure: A prologue and forty-two chapters mixing autobiography, doctrine, and scriptural commentary, with the author's own experience as the organizing proof.
meter_and_prosody: Latin prose, rhetorical and warm, with the psalm commentary woven in.
historical_context: Composed c. 1340–43 in the north of England, early in Rolle's hermit career, and later translated into Middle English (the Fire of Love); among the most widely read Latin spiritual works of the English fourteenth century.
literary_significance: The first major work of the English mystical tradition and the fountainhead of its characteristic language of warmth, sweetness, and song.
attribution_notes: Rolle's authorship secure.
bibliographical_notes: Standard edition: M. Deanesly (1915); trans. C. Wolters (1972).

title: Ego Dormio
alternative_titles: Ego Dormio et Cor Meum Vigilat
description: Richard Rolle's English epistle on the three degrees of love, written c. 1340 for a nun of Yedingham (or a recluse of his circle): a lyrical meditation, interspersed with the lyric 'My king that water grette', on the ascent from the love of God's creatures through the love of Christ's humanity to the highest love, which he describes as 'wonderful' — the experience he had felt at Hampole.
plot_or_argument: Taking its text from the Song of Songs ('I sleep and my heart wakes'), the epistle teaches the recipient the three degrees of love — insuperable, inseparable, singular — describes Rolle's own experience of heavenly song, and closes with the Passion meditation and the lyric of Christ's weeping for man's sin.
narrative_structure: A single epistle in three movements, with the inset lyric as its devotional climax.
meter_and_prosody: Rhythmical, alliterative prose with the lyric 'My king' in rhymed stanzas.
historical_context: Composed c. 1340 in Yorkshire, among Rolle's earliest English writings, for the guidance of a woman religious; preserved in numerous manuscripts, often with the other English epistles.
literary_significance: The classic statement of Rolle's three degrees of love and a key text of the early English mystical epistles.
attribution_notes: Rolle's authorship secure.
bibliographical_notes: Standard edition: S. J. Ogilvie-Thomson, EETS OS 293 (1988).

title: The Form of Living
description: Richard Rolle's English epistle of spiritual guidance, written c. 1348 for Margaret Kirkby, the anchoress of Ainderby, and the most influential of his English works: a rule of the devout life in twelve chapters, from the love of God and the practice of prayer through the discernment of true contemplation to the joy of the heavenly song. It became the classic handbook of English anchoresses after Ancrene Wisse.
plot_or_argument: Addressed to Margaret 'in the form of living', the epistle teaches the love of God above all things, the exercise of prayer and meditation on the Passion, the temptations and consolations of the solitary life, and the discernment of the true 'song' of contemplation from delusion.
narrative_structure: Twelve short chapters of practical and mystical instruction, in the epistle form of the Rolle canon.
meter_and_prosody: Rhythmical alliterative prose of the Rolle school.
historical_context: Written c. 1348 for Margaret Kirkby, recluse of Ainderby, in the last year of Rolle's life; the most widely copied of his English writings, it circulated into the fifteenth century and was printed by Wynkyn de Worde.
literary_significance: The bridge between Ancrene Wisse and the fifteenth-century devotional manuals, and the classic of the Rolle tradition in English.
attribution_notes: Rolle's authorship secure.
bibliographical_notes: Standard edition: S. J. Ogilvie-Thomson, EETS OS 293 (1988).

title: The Scale of Perfection
description: Walter Hilton's masterpiece, in two books: the first (c. 1380s) addresses an anchoress on the reformation of the soul in faith and the destruction of the image of sin; the second (c. 1390s), on the reformation of the soul in feeling, expounds the contemplative life and the discernment of true spiritual experience. The most systematic and influential English treatise on contemplation.
plot_or_argument: Book I anatomizes the soul's sinfulness and its reformation through faith, humility, and the practice of prayer, with the famous analysis of the image of sin to be broken down; Book II teaches the higher work of contemplation — the entry into the 'darkness' of unknowing, the gifts of the Holy Spirit, and the tests by which true spiritual experience may be known from false.
narrative_structure: Two books of graduated instruction (the 'scale'), moving from the active to the contemplative life, in the tradition of the spiritual ladder.
meter_and_prosody: Measured, precise prose, plainer than Rolle's and theologically more careful.
historical_context: Composed c. 1380–96 by the Augustinian canon Walter Hilton, for a woman recluse and for the devout laity; printed by Wynkyn de Worde (1494) and read by the English Benedictine revival of the seventeenth century.
literary_significance: The classic systematic treatise of English mysticism: its discrimination of true and false spiritual experience and its doctrine of the image of God shaped English devotional thought for three centuries.
attribution_notes: Hilton's authorship secure.
bibliographical_notes: Some forty manuscripts. Standard edition: T. Bestul, TEAMS (2000); J. P. H. Clark and R. Dorward (trans., 1991).

title: Epistle on the Mixed Life
description: Walter Hilton's epistle addressed to a wealthy layman, probably a lord, teaching the 'mixed life' — the life that joins the active works of mercy and the duties of estate with the inner practice of contemplation. It is the classic English statement that contemplation is not the preserve of monks: lay people in the world may and should live the contemplative life in their degree.
plot_or_argument: Hilton distinguishes three lives — active, contemplative, and mixed — and argues that the mixed life, combining works of charity and governance with prayer and meditation, is the life of prelates and devout lay lords; he then teaches his addressee the practice of this life in his daily affairs.
narrative_structure: A single epistle in two movements: the doctrine of the three lives, and its application to the recipient's estate.
meter_and_prosody: Plain, authoritative prose of the Hilton school.
historical_context: Composed c. 1385, when the growth of lay piety and the demand for vernacular guidance was transforming English religious life; preserved in numerous manuscripts, often with the Scale of Perfection.
literary_significance: The founding text of the 'mixed life' tradition that legitimized lay contemplation and shaped the spirituality of the fifteenth-century gentry.
attribution_notes: Hilton's authorship secure.
bibliographical_notes: Standard edition: S. J. Ogilvie-Thomson (1986).

title: Revelations of Divine Love
description: Julian of Norwich's account of the sixteen revelations ('showings') she received during a grave illness on 8 May 1373, in two versions — the Short Text written soon after, and the Long Text, the fruit of some twenty years of meditation, completed c. 1393. Its theology of divine love — 'all shall be well, and all manner of thing shall be well' — and of Jesus as mother makes it the greatest work of English mysticism and the first book in English known to be by a woman.
plot_or_argument: At the point of death, the thirty-year-old Julian receives a series of visions of Christ's Passion, the Virgin, the world's littleness (the hazelnut), and the Lord's meaning: that love is his meaning; the Long Text unfolds these showings into a theology of sin, suffering, divine motherhood, and the 'great deed' by which all shall be made well.
narrative_structure: Eighty-six (or more) chapters of vision, exposition, and prayer, organized by the order of the showings and the decades of their meditation.
principal_characters: Julian (visionary); Christ; the Virgin Mary; the fiend
meter_and_prosody: Plain, meditative prose of extraordinary depth; homely images (the hazelnut) carrying speculative theology.
historical_context: The showings occurred in Norwich on 8 May 1373; Julian became an anchoress at St Julian's church and wrote the Short Text shortly after and the Long Text c. 1393; Margery Kempe visited her c. 1413; the Long Text circulated in manuscript and in the printed editions of Serenus Cressy (1670).
literary_significance: The summit of the English mystical tradition: the first major theological work by an English woman, and a text of the first importance for the history of women's writing and of Christian theology.
attribution_notes: The author is known only as Julian of Norwich (from her church); her name in the world is unknown.
bibliographical_notes: Short Text: BL Additional MS 37790; Long Text: Paris, Bibliothèque nationale MS fonds anglais 40, etc. Standard edition: N. Watson and J. Jenkins (2006).

title: The Cloud of Unknowing
description: The classic English treatise of apophatic contemplation, written in the late fourteenth century by an anonymous master (perhaps a Carthusian or secular priest) for a young disciple: the soul seeking God must enter the 'cloud of unknowing' between itself and God, striking down every thought with the dart of longing love and the 'naked intent' of the single word. The most intellectually rigorous work of the English mystical canon.
plot_or_argument: The author teaches his disciple the work of contemplation: the forgetting of all creatures, the rejection of discursive meditation, the piercing of the darkness with love — and warns throughout against the false mysticism of physical fervour and deluded visions, prescribing the discipline of the single word ('God' or 'love') repeated in the heart.
narrative_structure: Seventy-five short chapters of graduated instruction, in the apophatic tradition of pseudo-Dionysius, with the 'cloud' as its organizing image.
principal_characters: the author (spiritual director); the young disciple (addressee)
meter_and_prosody: Precise, sinewy prose, paradoxically articulate about the ineffable; vivid negative imagery (clouds, darts, nakedness).
historical_context: Composed c. 1375–1400, probably in the north-east Midlands, in the orbit of the Carthusian order; it circulated with the author's other works (The Book of Privy Counselling, the translation of pseudo-Dionysius's Mystical Theology) and was read by the English Benedictine revival and by modern contemplatives (Thomas Merton).
literary_significance: The supreme English expression of the negative way and a work of the first rank in the European contemplative tradition; its psychology of attention and intention has given it a continuing modern readership.
attribution_notes: Anonymous; the author is often identified as a Carthusian on grounds of the work's transmission, but the identification is conjectural.
bibliographical_notes: Seventeen manuscripts. Standard edition: P. Hodgson, EETS OS 218 (1944); A. Spearing (trans., 2001).

title: The Mirror of the Blessed Life of Jesus Christ
description: Nicholas Love's English translation and adaptation of the pseudo-Bonaventuran Meditationes Vitae Christi, completed c. 1410: a life of Christ from the Annunciation to Pentecost, written for the 'simple' reader to make the humanity of Jesus present to the imagination, with meditations, prayers, and passages against Lollard positions. The most widely circulated devotional work of fifteenth-century England.
plot_or_argument: Following the gospel narrative day by day, the Mirror unfolds the life, ministry, Passion, and resurrection of Christ in vivid meditative episodes — the nativity, the sermons, the agony, the crucifixion as witnessed by Mary — each closed with moral application, and supplemented by Love's own anti-Wycliffite 'treatise on the sacrament'.
narrative_structure: A day-by-day meditation on the life of Christ in the Meditationes tradition, with the Passion as its affective centre and devotional prayers appended.
principal_characters: Christ; the Virgin Mary; the disciples
meter_and_prosody: Plain, warm prose of the Carthusian devotional school.
historical_context: Completed c. 1410 by Nicholas Love, Carthusian prior of Mount Grace, with the explicit approval of Archbishop Arundel as an orthodox counter to Lollard vernacular scripture; preserved in more manuscripts than any other Middle English devotional text and printed by Caxton (1484) and his successors.
literary_significance: The great bestseller of late medieval English devotion: it fixed the affective image of Christ's humanity for a century of English readers and is the key exhibit in the politics of vernacular theology after Arundel's Constitutions.
attribution_notes: Love's authorship secure (named in the work's memorial note).
bibliographical_notes: Some sixty-five manuscripts and early prints. Standard edition: M. G. Sargent (2005).

title: The Prick of Conscience
description: A northern poem of some 9,600 lines on the last things — the wretchedness of life, death, purgatory, the pains of hell and joys of heaven, and the day of doom — traditionally attributed to Richard Rolle but now generally denied to him. It was the most widely copied Middle English poem of all, surviving in more manuscripts than any other verse of the period, including Piers Plowman and the Canterbury Tales.
plot_or_argument: In seven parts the poem moves from the misery of human life through the certainty and terror of death to the topography of the afterlife — purgatory's cleansing fire, hell's torments, heaven's bliss — and the signs and terrors of the last judgement, closing with the exhortation to live so as to die well.
narrative_structure: A seven-part didactic sequence on the four last things, in the memento mori tradition, with the 'prick' of conscience as its titular image.
meter_and_prosody: Octosyllabic couplets in the northern dialect, plain and insistent.
historical_context: Composed c. 1350 in the north of England, in the pastoral tradition of the fourth Lateran council's emphasis on penance; preserved in over 120 manuscripts and translated into Latin (Stimulus Conscientiae); its popularity made it the period's standard popular eschatology.
literary_significance: The most widely read Middle English poem of its century and the great vernacular encyclopedia of the afterlife; its manuscript diffusion is a central fact of late medieval English literary culture.
attribution_notes: Attributed to Richard Rolle in many manuscripts, but modern scholarship rejects the attribution (Ralph Hanna and others); authorship_status reflects the dispute.
bibliographical_notes: Over 120 manuscripts. Standard edition: R. Morris (1863); J. H. Morey (2012).

title: Dives and Pauper
description: An anonymous prose treatise of c. 1405–10 in dialogue form on the Ten Commandments, in which the rich man Dives asks and the poor man Pauper answers — a vast compendium of moral theology, canon law, and social commentary, notable for its defence of poverty, its discussion of images and tithes, and its sympathy with reformist positions short of heresy. The great popular summa of fifteenth-century English orthodoxy.
plot_or_argument: Dives, the wealthy layman, poses the hard questions of Christian practice — the worship of images, oaths, tithes, usury, the duties of the rich to the poor — and Pauper, the poor and learned clerk, answers each with doctrine, law, and exemplum, through all ten commandments.
narrative_structure: A sustained catechetical dialogue in ten commandments, with the social argument between rich and poor as its dramatic engine.
meter_and_prosody: Plain, copious prose with Latin quotations translated for the lay reader.
historical_context: Composed c. 1405–10, in the aftermath of Arundel's Constitutions (1409), by a learned clerk conversant with both orthodox and reformist positions; printed by Pynson (1493) and read into the Reformation.
literary_significance: The most comprehensive vernacular treatment of the Decalogue in medieval England and a central witness to the social teaching of the late medieval church on wealth, poverty, and images.
attribution_notes: Anonymous; a Franciscan authorship has been conjectured.
bibliographical_notes: Twelve manuscripts. Standard edition: P. H. Barnum, EETS OS 275, 280, 323 (1976–2004).

title: Festial
description: John Mirk's cycle of English sermons for the feasts of the church year, composed c. 1380s at Lilleshall Abbey: lively, exemplum-rich homilies designed for parish priests to read to their congregations, from Advent through the temporale and sanctorale to the dedication of the church. The most popular sermon collection of late medieval England.
plot_or_argument: Each sermon expounds the day's feast — its history, its scripture, and its moral — with the miracle stories and exempla that made the Festial famous: the monk and the birds, the usurer's bees, the proud lady's punishment — and closes with practical instruction for the parish.
narrative_structure: A cycle of seventy-four (or more) sermons following the church year, in the homiletic-exemplary manner.
principal_characters: the exemplary figures of the tales
meter_and_prosody: Plain, animated prose with verse tags and exemplary narrative.
historical_context: Composed by the Augustinian canon John Mirk, prior of Lilleshall, in the 1380s, for the 'ignorant' parish clergy; it spread across England in some forty manuscripts and was printed by Caxton (1483) and repeatedly thereafter.
literary_significance: The classic of the English late medieval sermon and the principal record of orthodox parish preaching in the age of Lollardy; its exempla are a treasury of popular piety.
attribution_notes: Mirk's authorship secure (he names himself in the preface).
bibliographical_notes: Some forty manuscripts. Standard edition: S. Powell, EETS OS 334–335 (2009–11).

title: Legends of Holy Women
description: Osbern Bokenham's collection of thirteen verse lives of female saints, written 1443–47 at the request of a circle of East Anglian patrons, several of them women: Margaret, Anne, Christine, the Eleven Thousand Virgins, Faith, Agnes, Dorothy, Mary Magdalene, Katherine, Cecilia, Agatha, Lucy, and Elizabeth of Hungary. The major fifteenth-century English legendary of women's sanctity.
plot_or_argument: Each life narrates the saint's birth, conversion, and martyrdom (or holy death), with the debates, torments, and miracles of the genre; the framing prologues record the patrons who commissioned each legend, making the work a document of literary patronage as much as of hagiography.
narrative_structure: A sequence of independent verse legends, each with its own prologue naming the patron, in the Chaucerian-Lydgatean manner.
principal_characters: St Margaret; St Anne; St Katherine; St Mary Magdalene; St Cecilia; and the other saints; Bokenham (narrator)
meter_and_prosody: Couplets and rhyme royal in the Lydgatean style, aureate but warm.
historical_context: Composed 1443–47 by the Augustinian friar Osbern Bokenham of Stoke by Clare, Suffolk, for Lady Katherine Denston, Isabel Hunt, and other East Anglian gentry women; preserved in BL Arundel MS 327 (the author's own manuscript).
literary_significance: The principal fifteenth-century English collection of female saints' lives and a uniquely documented instance of women's literary patronage in the period.
attribution_notes: Bokenham's authorship secure; he names himself and his patrons throughout.
bibliographical_notes: BL Arundel MS 327. Standard edition: M. S. Serjeantson, EETS OS 206 (1938).

title: The Life of St Katharine
alternative_titles: Capgrave's Life of Saint Katharine of Alexandria
description: John Capgrave's verse life of St Katharine of Alexandria, composed c. 1445: the learned virgin's conversion, her debate with the fifty philosophers, her refusal of the emperor Maxentius, the wheels of her torture, and her mystical marriage to Christ. The most polished saint's life of the fifteenth century, in rhyme royal with an elaborate prologue.
plot_or_argument: Katharine, the learned princess of Alexandria, is converted by a hermit's vision of the Virgin and wedded to Christ; she confounds the emperor's philosophers in public debate, converts them and the empress, endures the wheels and the prison's angelic visits, and is beheaded — her body borne by angels to Sinai, where the milk, not blood, flows from her severed neck.
narrative_structure: Five books of hagiographical narrative, from birth and conversion through debate and passion to translation, in the classical five-book scheme.
principal_characters: St Katharine; the Emperor Maxentius; the fifty philosophers; the Virgin Mary; the hermit Adrian
meter_and_prosody: Rhyme royal stanzas of Lydgatean polish, with aureate diction and classical allusion.
historical_context: Composed c. 1445 by the Augustinian friar John Capgrave of Lynn, in the learned East Anglian tradition of Lydgate and Bokenham; the prologue places the poem in the line of Chaucer's Legend of Good Women; preserved in Bodleian Rawlinson Poet. 118 and Arundel MS 396.
literary_significance: The most accomplished Middle English life of St Katharine — the patron saint of learning — and the summit of fifteenth-century learned hagiography in verse.
attribution_notes: Capgrave's authorship secure (he names himself in the prologue).
bibliographical_notes: Bodleian Library, Rawlinson Poet. 118; Arundel MS 396. Standard edition: C. Horstmann, EETS OS 100 (1893); K. A. Winstead, TEAMS (1999).

title: The Book of Margery Kempe
description: The dictated spiritual autobiography of Margery Kempe of King's Lynn (c. 1436–38), commonly called the first autobiography in English: her conversion after childbirth, her marriage and vow of chastity, her uncontrollable weeping at the thought of the Passion, her pilgrimages to Jerusalem, Rome, and Santiago, and her examinations for heresy before the archbishops of Canterbury and York. A unique document of female lay piety and of fifteenth-century English life.
plot_or_argument: Margery recounts her visionary conversations with Christ, her struggle with her husband for chastity, her travels through Europe and the Holy Land, her clashes with hostile clergy and her vindications, her visit to Julian of Norwich, and her old age caring for her ailing husband — the whole narrated in the third person through her scribes.
narrative_structure: Two books of episodic autobiography, moving between mystical colloquy and the social world of East Anglian towns, courts, and pilgrim routes.
principal_characters: Margery Kempe; John Kempe (her husband); Julian of Norwich; Christ (in dialogue); the archbishops
meter_and_prosody: Direct, colloquial prose, vivid in dialogue and detail, mediated by her scribes.
historical_context: Dictated c. 1436–38, with a second book of the 1430s–40s, in the East Anglian culture of orthodox lay devotion shadowed by the Lollard trials; the complete text was lost until the discovery of the manuscript in 1934 (BL Additional MS 61823), and first published in 1936.
literary_significance: The first autobiography in English and the earliest extended account of a laywoman's religious life; its frankness about body, marriage, and authority has made it a founding text of women's literary history.
attribution_notes: Margery Kempe's authorship (by dictation to scribes) is recorded within the book itself.
bibliographical_notes: BL Additional MS 61823. Standard edition: S. B. Meech and H. E. Allen, EETS OS 212 (1940); B. Windeatt (trans., 1985).

title: Wycliffite Bible
description: The first complete translation of the Bible into English, produced in the circle of John Wyclif at Oxford and Lutterworth: the literal Early Version (c. 1382), associated with Nicholas of Hereford, and the idiomatic Later Version (c. 1388–95), associated with John Purvey. Banned by Archbishop Arundel's Constitutions (1409) but copied throughout the fifteenth century, it is the greatest monument of Lollard vernacular theology.
plot_or_argument: The translation renders the whole Vulgate — Old and New Testaments, with the apocrypha — into English, the Early Version word-for-word after the Latin, the Later Version in fluent, idiomatic prose, with prologues defending vernacular scripture and a general prologue expounding the Lollard program of 'poor priests' and scriptural preaching.
narrative_structure: The complete biblical canon in translation, with the characteristic Lollard prologues and glosses (in some manuscripts) as its apparatus.
meter_and_prosody: Prose: the Later Version in particular is a landmark of plain, idiomatic English style.
historical_context: Made c. 1382–95 in Wyclif's circle, condemned by the Blackfriars council (1382) and by Arundel's Constitutions (1409), which forbade unlicensed vernacular scripture; despite the ban, some 250 manuscripts survive, and the translation fed the English biblical tradition through Tyndale to the King James Version.
literary_significance: The foundational text of the English Bible: its phrasing passed into the sixteenth-century translations and into the common language of English devotion, and its very existence redefined the politics of vernacular religion.
attribution_notes: Traditionally called the 'Wycliffe Bible', but modern scholarship dissents from Wyclif's personal authorship; the translation is the work of his circle (Hereford, Purvey, and others). authorship_status reflects this traditional attribution.
bibliographical_notes: Some 250 manuscripts. Standard edition: J. Forshall and F. Madden, 4 vols (1850).

title: Twelve Conclusions of the Lollards
description: The Lollard manifesto of 1395, presented to parliament and nailed to the doors of Westminster Hall and St Paul's during its session: twelve conclusions denouncing the church's temporal lordship, clerical celibacy, transubstantiation, blessing of material things, clerical exemption, and the wars, crafts, and oaths by which the clergy sustain their power. The most famous document of English medieval dissent.
plot_or_argument: The conclusions move from the church's worldly dominion and the clergy's unworthy estate through the 'false miracle of the sacrament' to the 'unnecessary trades' (goldsmiths, armourers) that serve the church's pride, closing with the demand for a poor, preaching clergy and the renunciation of war and oaths.
narrative_structure: Twelve numbered propositions, each with its brief scriptural and logical support, in the petitionary form of a parliamentary bill.
meter_and_prosody: Plain, forceful English with Latin tags, in the Lollard plain style.
historical_context: Presented to parliament and posted at Westminster and St Paul's in 1395, in the political crisis of Richard II's reign; it provoked the orthodox counter-writings of Roger Dymmok and others and fixed the public image of Lollardy.
literary_significance: The founding manifesto of English religious dissent: its arguments against images, pilgrimage, and transubstantiation anticipate the Reformation by a century and a quarter.
attribution_notes: Anonymous (collective authorship in the Wycliffite movement).
bibliographical_notes: Preserved in Roger Dymmok's refutation and later copies. Standard edition: in Selections from English Wycliffite Writings, ed. A. Hudson (1978).

title: De Civili Dominio
description: John Wyclif's most explosive treatise (1375–76), expounding his doctrine of dominion: lordship is founded on grace, so that the sinful clergy — the pope included — forfeit their right to temporal possessions, and kings may and must strip the church of its wealth. The book that made Wyclif the theorist of disendowment and the target of papal condemnation.
plot_or_argument: Wyclif argues that all dominion derives from God and is held only by the righteous; the reprobate hold possessions unjustly; the clergy's endowment was conditional on their holiness and may be revoked by lay lords; and the English king, as God's vicar in his realm, is bound to reform and disendow the delinquent church.
narrative_structure: Three books of scholastic argument, from the metaphysics of dominion through its application to the church to the duties of the king.
meter_and_prosody: Latin prose in the Oxford scholastic manner, relentlessly syllogistic.
historical_context: Composed at Oxford and Lutterworth in 1375–76, when the papal-imperial politics of the Great Schism's prelude and the English crown's anti-papal statutes (Provisors, Praemunire) gave Wyclif's theories immediate political force; nineteen propositions from it were condemned by Gregory XI in 1377.
literary_significance: The theoretical charter of Lollardy's attack on ecclesiastical wealth and the most consequential political theology written in medieval England.
attribution_notes: Wyclif's authorship secure.
bibliographical_notes: Standard edition: Wyclif Society (J. Loserth, 1900–04).

title: The Repressor of Over Much Blaming of the Clergy
description: Reginald Pecock's great vernacular apologia (c. 1449–55), answering the Lollards' eleven 'blamings' of the clergy — against images, pilgrimages, clerical endowments, the pope, and the religious orders — not by authority but by the 'doom of reason'. The most original work of English theology between Wyclif and the Reformation, and the cause of its author's own condemnation.
plot_or_argument: Pecock restates the Lollard objections with scrupulous fairness and answers each by rational argument: faith is grounded in reason, images and pilgrimages serve the memory and the affections, clerical endowment is lawful when used rightly, and the church's hierarchy is the ordinance of God — while insisting, to his ruin, that the clergy must be judged by scripture and reason rather than by bare authority.
narrative_structure: Five parts answering the successive Lollard conclusions, in the dialectical form of objection and response.
meter_and_prosody: Plain English of argument, with an invented philosophical vocabulary ('unbileve', 'moral philosophi').
historical_context: Composed c. 1449–55 by the bishop of Chichester, in the controversy over vernacular theology after Arundel's Constitutions; Pecock's reliance on reason over authority led to his trial (1457), his abjuration at Paul's Cross, and the burning of his books.
literary_significance: The supreme monument of fifteenth-century English rational theology and a tragic witness to the church's fear of its own vernacular defenders.
attribution_notes: Pecock's authorship secure.
bibliographical_notes: Cambridge University Library MS Kk.4.26 (autograph). Standard edition: C. Babington, Rolls Series 19, 2 vols (1860).

title: The Book of Faith
description: Reginald Pecock's vernacular treatise of 1456 on the nature of faith and its relation to reason, written in the last years before his condemnation: faith, he argues, is a species of knowledge grounded in evidence and reason, not mere belief on authority — the doctrine that brought him to trial and abjuration. It survives in the author's own manuscript.
plot_or_argument: Pecock analyzes faith as intellectual assent produced by the 'doom of reason' on credible testimony, distinguishes it from opinion and knowledge, answers the objections of the 'unbilevers', and defends the lay person's right and duty to understand what he believes.
narrative_structure: Two books of philosophical-theological analysis, in the scholastic quaestio manner adapted to English.
meter_and_prosody: Argumentative English prose, technical and precise.
historical_context: Completed in 1456, a year before Pecock's trial; its rationalism was among the charges against him, and the work survives only in the Trinity College, Cambridge, autograph manuscript (MS B.14.45).
literary_significance: The boldest medieval English statement of the rationality of faith, and the terminus of vernacular theology before the Reformation.
attribution_notes: Pecock's authorship secure.
bibliographical_notes: Trinity College, Cambridge, MS B.14.45 (autograph). Standard edition: J. L. Morison (1909).

title: Polychronicon (Trevisa's translation)
description: John Trevisa's English translation of Ranulf Higden's Polychronicon, the universal history that dominated English historical reading: the world's geography, the history of Britain from the Britons to the fourteenth century, and the wonders of the world, in Trevisa's fluent, expansive prose, completed in 1387 for Thomas, Lord Berkeley. Printed by Caxton in 1482, it is the great English prose chronicle of the period.
plot_or_argument: Following Higden's seven books, the work describes the world and Britain, then narrates English history from the Britons and Saxons through the Norman kings to the reign of Edward III, with its famous prefatory Dialogue on Translation in which Trevisa defends the rendering of Latin learning into English.
narrative_structure: Seven books of world and British history, with Trevisa's Dialogue and the Berkeley continuations as its frame and sequel.
principal_characters: the kings and peoples of British history
meter_and_prosody: Prose: fluent, idiomatic, and expansive — a landmark of fourteenth-century English prose style.
historical_context: Completed in 1387 by Trevisa, chaplain of Thomas, Lord Berkeley, at Berkeley Castle; printed by Caxton (1482, with his continuation to 1460) and read into the sixteenth century.
literary_significance: The principal English universal history of the later Middle Ages and, with its Dialogue on Translation, a classic text of vernacular self-consciousness.
attribution_notes: Trevisa's authorship of the translation secure (named in the Berkeley manuscripts).
bibliographical_notes: Fourteen manuscripts. Standard edition: C. Babington and J. R. Lumby, Rolls Series 41, 9 vols (1865–86).

title: On the Properties of Things
description: John Trevisa's English translation of Bartholomaeus Anglicus's De proprietatibus rerum (On the Properties of Things), the great medieval encyclopedia of nature, man, and the cosmos, completed c. 1398–99: nineteen books from God and the angels through the elements, animals, and plants to the human body and soul. Printed by Wynkyn de Worde in 1495, it was the standard English encyclopedia for two centuries.
plot_or_argument: The work proceeds systematically through the orders of creation — God, angels, the soul, the elements, the heavens, birds, beasts, herbs, and the arts and sciences — describing each thing's properties and their moral and medical meanings, in a summa of medieval natural knowledge.
narrative_structure: Nineteen books of encyclopedic description, each subdivided by topic, in the tradition of Isidore and the thirteenth-century encyclopedists.
meter_and_prosody: Prose: Trevisa's learned yet idiomatic English, rich in technical vocabulary.
historical_context: Completed in 1398–99 at Berkeley, dedicated to Thomas, Lord Berkeley; printed by Wynkyn de Worde (c. 1495), when it served the medical and scientific reading of the Tudor period; Shakespeare drew on it.
literary_significance: The great English encyclopedia of the Middle Ages and the principal channel by which medieval natural science entered English prose.
attribution_notes: Trevisa's authorship of the translation secure (named in the text).
bibliographical_notes: BL Additional MS 27944; de Worde's print (1495). Standard edition: M. C. Seymour et al., 3 vols (1975–88).

title: The Brut Chronicle
description: The Middle English prose Brut, the most popular secular text in late medieval England: a chronicle of Britain from the Trojan Brutus through the Arthurian kings to the fourteenth century, with continuations carrying the story through the Wars of the Roses. Over 180 manuscripts survive in English — more than any other secular work — and Caxton's print (1480) made it the standard popular history of England.
plot_or_argument: The chronicle narrates the legendary British history of the Brut tradition — Brutus, Lear, Arthur — then the Saxon, Norman, and Plantagenet reigns, with the continuations adding the Lancastrian and Yorkist wars; its plain, annalistic prose made it the layman's history of England.
narrative_structure: A regnal chronicle in the Brut tradition, open-ended and continuously continued by successive compilers.
principal_characters: Brutus; Arthur; the kings of England to Edward IV
meter_and_prosody: Plain, formulaic prose of the chronicle tradition.
historical_context: The earliest version was made in the later fourteenth century, probably in London, from French and Latin sources; it was expanded continuously through the fifteenth century (the 'common version' to 1419, continuations to 1461 and later) and printed by Caxton in 1480.
literary_significance: The bestselling secular book of the English Middle Ages: its diffusion defines the popular historical culture out of which Tudor history writing grew.
attribution_notes: Anonymous and compilational.
bibliographical_notes: Over 180 English manuscripts. Standard edition: F. W. D. Brie, EETS OS 131, 136 (1906–08).

title: Mandeville's Travels
alternative_titles: The Voyage and Travels of Sir John Mandeville
description: The Book of Sir John Mandeville, the most popular travel book of the Middle Ages: a compilation, originally in French (c. 1357), of pilgrimage routes to Jerusalem, the marvels of Asia, the lands of Prester John, and the wonders of the East, framed by the persona of an English knight of St Albans whose travels are largely fictive. Its Middle English versions (from c. 1375) circulated more widely than any other travel narrative.
plot_or_argument: The narrator describes the way to Jerusalem and the holy places, then the farther East — Egypt, India, Cathay, the isles of the East — collecting marvels (the vegetable lamb, the phoenix, the fountain of youth), the palace of Prester John, and the customs of strange peoples, in a geography poised between pilgrimage, wonder, and imperial fantasy.
narrative_structure: An itinerary organized by regions and routes, with the pilgrimage to Jerusalem as its centre and the marvels of the East as its circumference.
principal_characters: Sir John Mandeville (persona); Prester John; the Great Khan
meter_and_prosody: Prose: plain, fluent, and endlessly translatable; the English versions descend from the French via Latin.
historical_context: Composed in French c. 1357, probably by a clerk in Liège or northern France using genuine itineraries and encyclopedias; translated into English from c. 1375 in several versions (the 'Defective' version foremost); printed by Wynkyn de Worde (1496); Columbus and Raleigh read it.
literary_significance: The great medieval bestseller of travel and wonder, and a foundational text of the European imagination of the East — read by explorers into the seventeenth century.
attribution_notes: Anonymous; the 'Sir John Mandeville' persona is generally regarded as fictional.
bibliographical_notes: Some 300 manuscripts in many languages. Standard edition: M. C. Seymour, EETS OS 319 (2002).

title: Paston Letters
description: The correspondence and papers of the Paston family of Norfolk, spanning 1422–1509: over a thousand letters, wills, and memoranda recording the family's rise from yeoman stock to gentry status, their lawsuits (above all the struggle for Caister Castle), their marriages, and the texture of fifteenth-century provincial life. The richest surviving archive of medieval English family letters.
plot_or_argument: The letters move among the three generations of Pastons — the judge William, his sons John I and John II, their wives Margaret and Margery — and their circle: the siege of Caister, John II's life at court, Margery's secret marriage, the boys' schooling, and the daily business of land, law, and loyalty in East Anglia.
narrative_structure: An epistolary archive, not a composed work: its order is chronological and documentary, spanning the reigns of Henry VI, Edward IV, and Henry VII.
principal_characters: William Paston; Margaret Paston; John Paston I; John Paston II; Margery Paston; the family's servants and opponents
meter_and_prosody: Prose: the varied, idiomatic English of a literate gentry family, from Margaret's dictated letters to John II's courtier prose.
historical_context: Written 1422–1509 by the Norfolk Pastons, whose archive passed to the Earl of Yarmouth and was edited by John Fenn (1787); it documents the Wars of the Roses from the perspective of a gentry family and is a primary source for the period's social history.
literary_significance: The first great English family letter collection: a unique window on the language, law, and life of fifteenth-century England, and the ancestor of the English epistolary tradition.
attribution_notes: Collaborative (many family members and correspondents); authorship_status reflects the archive's collective character.
bibliographical_notes: BL Additional MSS 27443–27447, etc. Standard edition: N. Davis, Paston Letters and Papers of the Fifteenth Century, 3 vols, EETS SS 20–22 (1971–2004).

title: Cely Letters
description: The business correspondence of the Cely family, London wool merchants of the Staple of Calais, 1472–88: some 250 letters and papers recording the wool trade, shipping, politics, and daily life of a merchant family in the age of Edward IV and Richard III. The most vivid surviving record of English commercial life in the fifteenth century.
plot_or_argument: The letters pass between the brothers Robert, Richard, and George Cely in London and Calais and their factors, recording the buying and shipping of wool, prices and freights, news of the wars in France and at home (including the fall of Richard III), and the family's hunting, hawking, and domestic affairs.
narrative_structure: A documentary archive of business correspondence, chronological in arrangement, spanning sixteen years.
principal_characters: George Cely; Richard Cely the elder and younger; William Maryon; the Calais factors
meter_and_prosody: Prose: brisk, practical mercantile English, of great linguistic value.
historical_context: Written 1472–88, when the Celys' Calais staple stood at the centre of England's wool economy; discovered in 1860 among the family's papers and edited by H. E. Malden (1900).
literary_significance: The classic document of fifteenth-century English commerce and the merchant's English, complementing the Paston archive's gentry perspective.
attribution_notes: Collaborative (family and factors); authorship_status reflects the archive's collective character.
bibliographical_notes: Public Record Office, C.47/37 (now The National Archives, SC 1). Standard edition: A. Hanham, EETS OS 273 (1975).

title: The Book of St Albans
alternative_titles: The Book of Hawking, Hunting, and Heraldry
description: The gentleman's handbook printed at St Albans in 1486: treatises in verse and prose on hawking, hunting, and heraldry, together with the terms of venery and the 'companies of beasts', traditionally attributed to Dame Juliana Berners, prioress of Sopwell. It is the classic English manual of the gentleman's arts, reprinted and expanded into the seventeenth century.
plot_or_argument: The book instructs the reader in the falconer's and hunter's crafts — the mews, the lure, the chase of the hart, the terms of the hunt — and in the blazoning of arms, closing with the famous catalogues of collective nouns ('a parliament of rooks', 'a murmuration of starlings') that fixed the English vocabulary of the field.
narrative_structure: A compilation of distinct treatises (hawking; hunting; arms; blazoning) in the practical-manual tradition.
literary_form: courtesy book and household manual (verse and prose)
meter_and_prosody: Mixed: the hawking and hunting treatises in rhyme royal and couplets, the heraldry in prose.
historical_context: Printed at the schoolmaster press of St Albans in 1486 (a colophon names 'the schoolmaster of St Albans'), in the post-Caxton provincial print boom; the attribution to Juliana Berners appears in the 1496 de Worde reprint.
literary_significance: The foundational English manual of the gentleman's arts: its venery terms entered the language and its heraldry shaped Tudor and Stuart practice.
attribution_notes: Attributed to Dame Juliana Berners (prioress of Sopwell) in the 1496 reprint; the attribution is traditional and doubted. authorship_status reflects this traditional attribution.
bibliographical_notes: St Albans print (1486). Standard edition: R. Hands (1975).

title: The Forme of Cury
description: The earliest English cookery collection: some 200 recipes compiled c. 1390 by the master cooks of King Richard II, from potages and roasted meats to the subtleties and spiced dishes of the royal table, including the first English recipe for pasta ('macrows') and dishes with olive oil. It is the foundation document of English culinary literature.
plot_or_argument: The collection proceeds from the 'furmenty' and potages through flesh and fish days to the elaborate final courses, with the spices of the East (saffron, cloves, mace) and the French culinary vocabulary of the court marking the recipes' royal provenance.
narrative_structure: A recipe collection in the medieval cookbook tradition, organized by course and occasion, with the royal headnote claiming its authority.
meter_and_prosody: Prose: terse, practical recipe English with French technical terms.
historical_context: Compiled c. 1390 by the chief master cooks of Richard II, and preserved in the manuscript BL Additional MS 5016 (with the closely related manuscripts of the Curye on Inglysch group); first printed by Samuel Pegge (1780).
literary_significance: The first English cookbook and the classic document of medieval English courtly cuisine; its recipes are still cooked by food historians today.
attribution_notes: Anonymous (compiled by the king's cooks).
bibliographical_notes: BL Additional MS 5016. Standard edition: C. B. Hieatt and S. Butler, Curye on Inglysch, EETS SS 8 (1985).

title: The Babees Book
description: The classic late medieval courtesy book: a poem of instruction for young boys ('babees') entering noble households, teaching them how to stand, dress, serve at table, and speak to their betters, with the companion courtesy poems and John Russell's Boke of Nurture that accompany it in the manuscripts. The standard English manual of the civility that defined the late medieval and early modern gentleman.
plot_or_argument: The poem addresses the boy entering service, prescribing his conduct from rising to bedtime — cleanliness, table manners, deference of speech and gesture — and moralizing the discipline of courtesy as the school of virtue, in the tradition of the medieval courtesy literature descended from the classical 'nurture' of the young.
narrative_structure: A single didactic poem in the courtesy tradition, with the companion poems (Urbanitatis, Stans Puer ad Mensam, Russell's Boke of Nurture) forming a curriculum in the manuscripts.
meter_and_prosody: Couplets and seven-line stanzas, plain and mnemonic.
historical_context: Composed c. 1475, when the great households' demand for trained service and the school curriculum of manners converged; preserved in BL Harley MS 5086 and related manuscripts; edited by F. J. Furnivall (1868) in the volumes that founded the study of English manners literature.
literary_significance: The classic English courtesy book and the ancestor of the early modern conduct tradition (Erasmus, Castiglione's English imitators); its rules of table and speech chart the history of English civility.
attribution_notes: Anonymous.
bibliographical_notes: BL Harley MS 5086. Standard edition: F. J. Furnivall, EETS OS 32 (1868).
